exam: You are on a ward when a 45‑year‑old man collapses with no pulse. What is your first step? — Immediate CPR and defibrillation; do not wait for ECG.
A patient with known rheumatic heart disease presents with sudden collapse. What is the most likely arrhythmia? — Ventricular fibrillation secondary to scar tissue.
You have a patient with hypokalaemia presenting with palpitations. Which drug should you avoid? — Lidocaine, as it worsens hypokalaemic arrhythmias.
A 30‑year‑old woman with HIV presents with sudden chest pain and collapse. What investigation is most critical? — 12‑lead ECG to detect VT/VF.
You suspect sudden cardiac death due to acute MI. Which lab value confirms myocardial injury? — Troponin rise >3× upper limit.
A patient survives an episode of VF. What long‑term therapy should you consider? — Implantable cardioverter‑defibrillator if EF ≤30% and resources allow.
You find a normal ECG in a patient who collapsed. What could explain this? — The arrhythmia may have terminated spontaneously or the ECG missed the event.
You are in a rural clinic with no defibrillator. What is the best immediate action for a sudden collapse? — Start CPR and call for emergency transport; use a manual defibrillator if available.
ai.title: Sudden Cardiac Death
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A life‑threatening arrhythmic event that occurs within an hour of symptom onset. In low‑resource settings, common triggers include untreated ischemia, electrolyte imbalance, and rheumatic heart disease. Rapid recognition and basic resuscitation are essential.

b: Unwitnessed death within 24h of last seen alive
Witnessed collapse with no pulse and no response to CPR
sections.p: Sudden cardiac death is the unexpected loss of life due to a cardiac arrhythmia, usually ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia, occurring within one hour of symptom onset or unwitnessed death within 24 hours of last known well.

t.b: Shows ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation; absence of P waves and QRS complexes in VF
Elevated levels indicate myocardial injury; a rise >3× upper limit suggests acute MI as a precipitant

b: Immediate survival if defibrillation within 3–5 minutes
sections.p: SCD is an acute event; staging is not applicable. Prognosis depends on underlying disease and time to defibrillation.

b: Acute MI (most common in urban areas)
Rheumatic heart disease (valvular lesions causing arrhythmia)
Hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia (often from diarrhoea or herbal remedies)
sections.p: In East Africa and similar settings, the leading causes are acute coronary syndromes, electrolyte disturbances, and rheumatic heart disease. Other important contributors include HIV‑related cardiomyopathy, malaria‑induced myocarditis, and herbal cardiotoxins.

b: Chest pain or dyspnoea before collapse
sections.p: Patients may have a sudden loss of consciousness, chest pain, palpitations, or a witnessed collapse. In many cases, there are no preceding symptoms.
Prioritise life‑saving tests that are available locally. When advanced imaging is unavailable, rely on bedside ECG and basic labs.

t.b: VF shows chaotic baseline; VT shows wide QRS complexes
A rise >3× upper limit is significant
K+ <3.5 mmol/L or Mg2+ <0.7 mmol/L are dangerous
Signs of heart failure may hint at underlying cardiomyopathy

b: No pulse after 2 minutes of CPR
sections.p: Immediate cardiac arrest, cardiogenic shock, and pulmonary oedema are life‑threatening complications.

b: Immediate defibrillation with 200 J biphasic or 360 J monophasic if available
sections.p: Treat the arrhythmia first, then address the underlying cause. Use drugs that are safe in low‑resource settings and avoid those with high toxicity.

t.b: Avoid in patients with thyroid disease or pulmonary fibrosis
Avoid in patients with liver disease or severe renal impairment

sections.p: After survival, investigate for structural heart disease, manage risk factors, and consider implantable cardioverter‑defibrillator (ICD) if feasible.

t.b: EF <35% indicates high risk of recurrence

b: Neuro‑cardiogenic syncope – brief loss of consciousness with rapid recovery
sections.p: Syncope from neuro‑cardiogenic causes, pulmonary embolism, and seizures can mimic sudden collapse.

b: VF may be transient and not captured on ECG
sections.p: Normal ECG in early VF can be missed; low troponin may not rule out MI in chronic disease.
